title: Our production AI cost $3.42. Our CI cost $224.77 in 17 days.
audience: Founders, CTOs and operators budgeting for AI automation in a small business
hook: By mid-October, our production AI ledger showed $3.42 in total model spend. CI cost $224.77 in the first 17 days of the month.
problem: We suspected our AI features were leaking money. A small business can't carry a mystery bill, and guessing leads to cutting the wrong thing.
context: RachelOS runs lead capture and follow-up for a working South Florida real estate business. AI coding agents help build it, so it merges a lot of small pull requests (439 in one two-week stretch this fall), and every one runs the full test suite.
failedApproach: The obvious move was to cut model usage: cheaper models, fewer AI features. It would have saved almost nothing.
insight: So we stopped guessing and put two ledgers side by side
mechanics: Every production model call writes a ledger row (workload, model, tokens, cost) before the API key is even read, so total AI spend is one query.
GitHub's org billing report showed where the money actually went: 40,823 Linux minutes from October 1 to 17, nearly all of it CI.
We moved CI's test jobs to self-hosted runners in a Linux VM on a Mac we already own. Releases, migrations and anything else that touches production stay on GitHub's hosted runners.
We stopped the CMS project from rebuilding on commits that never touched it.

claims.text: Vercel: $6.49/day down to $2.47/day over the same windows, almost all of it build minutes.
Model spend recorded in the production ledger as of Oct 17: $3.42 in total ($3.35 Sonnet, $0.07 Haiku).

outcome.gap: The after window is only four days, and the Mac's electricity and wear aren't in the comparison. Database cost still needs a reading from the Neon console.

takeaway: Before you cut an AI feature to save money, put its ledger next to your CI bill. For us, the model was the cheapest part of the system.

cta.text: How RachelOS is built, in more detail: first comment.

evidence.summary: Cost before/after comment from Vercel /v1/billing/charges and the GitHub org billing usage API: Vercel $6.49 to $2.47/day (build CPU minutes), Actions $17.27 to $2.33/day (self-hosted runners).
Second-opinion audit: Actions $224.77 net for Oct 1–17 (40,823 Linux minutes); production AI ledger lifetime cost $3.35 Sonnet and $0.07 Haiku.
CI static, tests, app and build jobs moved to self-hosted runners in a Colima Ubuntu VM; release, Preview and migration workflows that hold production secrets stay GitHub-hosted.
439 pull requests merged between 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-12, counted with gh pr list.

sensitivity.notes: Infrastructure cost is Todd's to disclose. No lead, customer or revenue data.

commercial.rationale: Buyers of a governed AI build worry about runaway AI cost; this shows measured cost discipline on a live system.

title: We deleted 6,654 lines of release process and shipped faster
audience: Engineering leaders, delivery and transformation leads, CTOs of small teams
hook: We deleted 6,654 lines of release process. Time from pull request to production fell from 34 minutes to 22.
problem: Every safety step we'd added to the release path made sense on its own. Together they made me the operator: approval PRs, a separate migration lane, evidence refreshes, and labels that had quietly become shipping dependencies.
context: The system runs a live business, so release safety isn't optional. But a process that only works when its owner babysits it isn't safe. It just moves the risk to whoever is tired.
failedApproach: Each incident got a new gate. By October, 100 of 172 open issues were routed as high risk even though they all shipped through the same lane, and serial CI took a median 11.95 minutes before anything else could run.
insight: We kept exactly one human decision and automated everything around it
mechanics: When Preview checks pass, I get a 'Release ready' email linking to a page that lists the changes and any database migration in plain English.
One tap proves a database restore point exists, applies migrations, fast-forwards main, and runs production smoke tests and canaries.
We retired the approval PR and the separate migration lane, dropped main's duplicate CI run, and deleted tests that only checked file contents.
We gave the AI coding agents a written rule: no new gates unless the owner asks for one.

claims.text: PR opened to released: 34.07 minutes before, 22.15 after, owner wait included.
CI runner minutes per release: 42.62 before, 34.25 after.
Ten PRs removed 34 files and 6,654 lines, and closed 26 issues.
The next ordinary product PR merged itself 7.03 minutes after it opened, with zero commands from me.

outcome.gap: That's one before/after pair, not a trend, and we didn't claim dollar savings from it.

takeaway: If every incident adds a gate, the process eventually needs a full-time operator. Keep the one decision a human should make, and automate the rest.

cta.text: The full RachelOS write-up, release lane included, is in the first comment.

evidence.summary: Measured implementation proof for the development-system simplification: PR opened to RELEASED 34.07 vs 22.15 minutes; core runner job-minutes 42.62 vs 34.25; main's duplicate CI removed.
Final normal-product proof: PR #1045 merged automatically 7.03 minutes after opening with zero owner commands; remediation was ten PRs, 34 deleted files, 6,654 removed lines, 26 issues closed.

Diagnosis: 100 of 172 open issues routed HIGH on the same delivery lane; serial CI median 11.95 minutes; five structural causes including retired approval machinery and labels acting as shipping dependencies.
One release lane: the approval PR and the separate migration lane retired (+495/-2,882).
Agent contract: 'No new gates' rule and the one-tap release steps (CI check, restore point, migrations, fast-forward main, production smoke and canaries).

commercial.rationale: Delivery and transformation leaders live with governance that has outgrown its purpose; this is a measured example of finding and removing the constraint.

title: 966 merged pull requests and the conveyor that checks them
audience: CTOs, engineering managers and founders adopting AI coding agents
hook: The software behind our two-person real estate business has merged 966 pull requests since September 2025. This is the system that checks them before they reach production.
problem: AI coding agents can open pull requests faster than one person can review them. Either the human becomes the bottleneck, or review quietly stops happening.
context: This system handles real leads and real customer email, so moving fast can't mean merging anything.
insight: We treat agents as roles, not vendors, and every change rides the same conveyor
mechanics: Work starts from a GitHub issue with acceptance criteria. A deterministic script, not a model, routes it by risk.
One agent implements on its own branch and runs the same verification CI runs before opening the PR.
An independent reviewer checks the exact commit against the issue. Green CI plus a passing review merges automatically; a Draft PR is a hold.
Merging isn't releasing. Production only moves when I tap Release.
The review job and the model worker both run on hardware we own, so review doesn't consume hosted CI minutes.

claims.text: 966 merged PRs, 1,257 test files and 152 database migrations since the first commit on September 30, 2025.
Full local verification before a recent PR: 917 Jest suites, 14,260 tests and 278 browser tests passed.

outcome.gap: Volume isn't quality. An October audit found four production regressions that landed during a nine-day window of 300+ merges and were caught by production errors, not CI. That's the next thing to fix.

takeaway: With AI agents, code stops being the scarce resource. Verification you trust and a human decision you actually make are what's scarce now.

cta.text: If you're running coding agents in production, I'd like to hear how you handle review. What's working?

evidence.summary: Agent contract: issue-first work, deterministic routing (npm run route:issue), PR to CI to independent review to automatic merge, Draft means hold, merging is not a release, local launchd-supervised review worker.
GitHub GraphQL merged PR totalCount 966; first commit 2025-09-30; origin/dev ab1ea0a28 holds 1,257 test files and 152 migrations.
PR verification block: npm run verify:agent exited 0 with 917 Jest suites, 14,260 tests and 278 Playwright tests passing.
Audit risk 3: regressions #1813, #1814, #1837 and #1840 landed in a nine-day window of 300+ merges and were found by production errors, not CI.
DEC-189: agents are roles (primary, second opinion), not vendors; one agent per issue.

sensitivity.notes: Process description only; do not name the review model or provider accounts.

commercial.rationale: Shows a governed, human-decided AI delivery system working at volume, which is what the governed AI build sells.

title: The AI safety switch that silently turned off lead enrichment for three weeks
audience: Engineers and operators running AI in production
hook: For three weeks our lead-enrichment AI didn't run. Nothing crashed. The budget guard was doing exactly what we told it to.
problem: Every production AI call must carry a budget policy, and a call without one is refused before it reaches the provider. That's fail-closed, which is what you want for spend.
context: From September 18 our enrichment calls had no policy. They were refused, cost nothing and were logged, which is exactly why nobody noticed.
failedApproach: We treated no spend as no problem. The refusals sat in a ledger that no person was looking at.
insight: A fail-closed control needs an alarm as loud as the failure it prevents
mechanics: Every attempt is written to a ledger before the API key is read, so refusals can be counted after the fact.
Reading that ledger during a cost audit is how the refusals surfaced: every one rejected with AI_BUDGET_POLICY_MISSING, none reaching the provider.
From October 9 the calls ran again under a configured policy.

claims.text: 1,263 refused calls between September 18 and October 9, at a cost of $0.
From October 9 to the audit on October 17: 222 successful calls, $0.07 in total.

outcome.gap: We haven't measured what three weeks without enrichment cost in follow-up quality.

takeaway: Fail-closed is the right default for spend and for sending. But a refusal nobody sees is an outage that never pages anyone.

cta.text: Worth checking this week: how many calls did your AI guardrails refuse last month, and who would have found out?

evidence.summary: Production ai_execution_attempts read with the read-only role: claude-haiku-4-5 1,263 attempts 09-18 to 10-09, all rejected AI_BUDGET_POLICY_MISSING, never contacted; claude-haiku-5-5 222 attempts from 10-09, $0.07.
Attempt ledger migration; the audit notes the row is written before the credential is read, so the ledger is complete for the app.

sensitivity.notes: Aggregate call counts only. Confirm with Todd that the October 9 change was the policy before publishing.

commercial.rationale: Keeping a governed AI system observable after launch is the Operate & Improve retainer's job; this is the failure it prevents.

title: Our pre-send check unsubscribed the people it was checking
audience: Engineers and technical founders who send email from their own systems
hook: Our pre-send safety check unsubscribed 57 people. It was checking that their unsubscribe links worked.
problem: A campaign preflight visited every link in each rendered email to catch broken URLs, including each recipient's own unsubscribe link.
context: Unsubscribe is the one action you can't get wrong in either direction: wrongly suppressing someone silently stops their mail, and wrongly re-adding someone breaks a promise.
failedApproach: The unsubscribe route changed state on GET. Next.js answers a HEAD request by running GET, so even a 'harmless' HEAD check unsubscribed the recipient, and the send then failed on the suppression the check had just created.
insight: The code fix was small. Proving exactly who was affected was the real work
mechanics: Unsubscribing now changes state only on POST.
We identified the affected contacts by causal pairing, not a time window: an unsubscribe event followed within 0.13–0.67 seconds by that same contact's send failing on suppression.
The repair ran from a frozen list, never a fresh query, and wrote a recovery marker on every restored record.
A hard cutoff at the fix time means any later unsubscribe is treated as genuine and never auto-restored.

claims.text: 57 false unsubscribes confirmed across three campaigns, August 12–19.
A later read-only review of every suppressed contact found 0 remaining high- or medium-confidence false suppressions.

outcome.gap: Four suppressed contacts have no unsubscribe event at all. How they were suppressed is still unknown, so they were deliberately left alone.

takeaway: Anything that follows links will eventually follow yours: link checkers, email security scanners, prefetchers. Never change state on GET, and repair data from a frozen list with a marker on every row.

cta.text: If you send email from your own app, it's worth five minutes to check whether your unsubscribe route changes anything on GET.

evidence.summary: DEC-113 context: INC-2026-08-PREFLIGHT falsely unsubscribed 57 contacts through a bare UPDATE; the repair had to reconstruct intent from lead_events.

Contactability after the incident: repair rows carry a preflight_false_unsubscribe_repair marker; read-only classification found 0 high and 0 medium confidence cases, 15 true opt-outs, 4 with insufficient evidence left alone; INCIDENT_FIX_AT is a hard cutoff.

Mechanism: preflight probed every href including the unsubscribe link; the route mutated on GET and Next.js serves HEAD via GET; forensic signature was unsubscribe followed by EMAIL_SUPPRESSED within 0.13–0.67 seconds.

sensitivity.notes: These were Rachel's contacts and campaigns. Aggregate counts only; no contact, campaign or property names.

commercial.rationale: Shows production discipline around permission and data repair, which technical buyers check before trusting a build.

title: One shortlist, three emails: keys that described the visit, not the message
hook: A prospect got the same email three times in 12 minutes. Every system involved did exactly what it was told.
problem: A 'your community matches' email went out three times to one person, all three listing the same communities.
context: Duplicate email erodes trust fast, and we had duplicate protection.
failedApproach: It never fired. The protection was keyed on things that changed every time, and this email's code path skipped it entirely.
insight: Three independent failures had to line up
mechanics: The email provider's idempotency key included a submission counter, so each attempt minted a new key and the provider correctly sent each one. The key described the visit, not the message.
Our signed links embed an expiry timestamp, so every render produced a unique body and the content-hash dedupe could never match.
This receipt's code path had never been wired into the send ledger at all.
The fix allows one customer send per logical communication, keyed on business meaning, with volatile signed tokens normalized out before hashing. An invariant test suite pins it.

claims.text: Before the fix, nine recipients received 14 excess emails; 12 were this receipt, 18% of its 66 sends.
Found, fixed and documented within a day, September 8–9.

takeaway: Before you trust a hash or an idempotency key, ask what changes on every render. Key on intent, not on the event.

cta.text: A five-minute check for anyone sending email from their own code: what goes into your idempotency key?

evidence.summary: INC-2026-09-DUPLICATE-RECEIPT: one logical communication sent three times; nine recipients, 14 excess emails, 12 on the recommendation receipt (18% of 66); three independent failures required.
fix(email): enforce one customer send per logical communication intent; adds duplicateSendInvariant.test.ts and volatile-token normalization in contentDeliveryLedger.ts.

sensitivity.notes: Rachel's prospects. Never quote names, addresses or community lists from the incident record, which contains identifiers.

commercial.rationale: Accountable follow-up is half the build offer; a concrete duplicate-send fix is credible proof for technical evaluators.

title: We built the content machine before we knew content worked
audience: Founders and operators deciding what to build next
hook: In two weeks we merged 439 pull requests. 40% went to content tooling. 6% went to conversion, analytics and follow-up.
problem: The constraint in the business was turning inquiries into conversations, not producing more content.
context: Content tooling is satisfying to build and easy to demo. Connecting search analytics and tightening follow-up is less fun, and it's closer to revenue.
failedApproach: We kept extending the newsroom (briefs, evidence checks, CMS publishing, photo pipelines) before search analytics could tell us whether organic search was worth it.
insight: Count what you actually built, by category, before planning the next sprint
mechanics: We bucketed every PR merged from September 28 to October 12 by title: 176 content and media, 97 release and CI, 57 operator screens, 26 conversion, analytics and nurture.
We set that against where inquiries actually stall, which is before a real conversation happens.
The review recommended pausing content-machine expansion until analytics shows organic search pays.

claims.text: 439 merged PRs: 40% content tooling, 22% release and CI, 13% operator screens, 6% conversion and follow-up.

outcome.gap: Keyword buckets are approximate, and we haven't fully followed our own advice yet. Whether shifting effort moves conversion is still unmeasured.

takeaway: Your merge history is a budget. Read it like one before you plan the next sprint.

cta.text: Try it on your own repo: bucket the last two weeks of merged work and compare it with where customers actually drop off.

evidence.summary: Title-keyword classification of 439 PRs merged 2026-09-28 to 10-12: content/CMS/media 176, release/CI/review 97, operator 57, conversion/analytics/nurture 26, other 83.
Read-only strategy review of open issues recommended pausing content-machine expansion until Search Console and GA4 are connected and channel diagnosis shows organic is worth it.

sensitivity.notes: Engineering allocation only. Do not add lead counts, reply rates or conversion figures without Rachel's consent.

commercial.rationale: The diagnostic sells exactly this discipline: find the real constraint before building more.

title: The software worked. The workflow didn't.
audience: Small-business owners, real estate professionals and anyone building tools for a partner
hook: I built a lead system for my wife's real estate business: a ranked daily queue, drafted follow-ups, a morning briefing. She works from a printed call sheet and her own phone. She isn't wrong.
problem: The conversations were happening, but the system never heard about them, so it couldn't learn who was ready or what worked.
context: Rachel is the licensed agent. The calls, tours and judgment are hers. My job is making follow-up hard to drop.
failedApproach: My instinct was to build more screens. Every new operator feature assumed she would open the app, and she doesn't need to.
insight: Recording, not features, is the bottleneck, so the system has to meet her where she already works
mechanics: Print-friendly call sheets and text-message prompts instead of another dashboard.
One-word replies by text to record what happened, instead of a form.

outcome.gap: We don't know yet whether meeting her in print and text raises recorded conversations. That's the measurement we're setting up now.

takeaway: If the person you're building for works around your software, the software has the problem.

cta.text: Anyone else building tools for a spouse, partner or co-founder? What did you learn?

evidence.summary: Rachel works from a printed call sheet and texts leads from her personal phone, outside the system; outcomes go unrecorded as a result.
Read-only production audit of the action loop. Internal only: its counts describe Rachel's lead handling and are not for publication.

sensitivity.notes: Rachel approves the wording about her workflow. Confirm both mechanics are live before publishing. Never publish lead counts, response times or conversion figures in this note.

commercial.rationale: Brand differentiation for the founder story; the strongest human-versus-automation material we have.

title: My AI agent spent $237 watching CI
audience: Founders and engineers using cloud AI agents
hook: A cloud AI agent spent $237 of credit in about two days. Most of it went to watching CI and doing nothing.
problem: I set a cloud agent session to watch pull requests and re-check them on a schedule.
context: The pipeline already merged green PRs on its own. The watcher added nothing but wake-ups.
failedApproach: Reminder routines, a daily routine and every GitHub event on watched PRs each woke the session: about 27 wake-ups in 40 minutes, nearly all no-ops.
insight: Agents bill for attention, so don't give them attention they don't need
mechanics: Open the PR, hand off, and stop. Act only if it goes red.
Implementation runs in local sessions, not in a cloud sandbox.
If a follow-up check is truly needed, one scheduled task, not a chain of routines.

claims.text: $237 of a $250 cloud credit used in about two days.

outcome.gap: We haven't measured the month after the change yet.

takeaway: With agentic tools, idle attention is often the expensive part, not model quality. Budget wake-ups the way you'd budget API calls.

cta.text: Curious what others have found: where did your agent spend actually go?

evidence.summary: One cloud session woken by about six reminder routines, a daily routine and every event on watched PRs (around 27 wakes in 40 minutes); $237 of $250 credit gone in about two days. Needs a billing export before the number is published.

commercial.rationale: Operators adopting agents need cost hygiene; this is a relatable, specific example.

title: What relocating buyers ask before they ever call an agent
audience: Buyers and sellers relocating to South Florida, and referral partners in feeder markets
hook: Before buyers moving to South Florida ever talk to me, they've already told us their budget and timeline. What they ask next tells you what actually worries them.
problem: Relocating buyers carry questions they don't ask out loud until late, and late answers cost them options.
context: Our home-match questionnaire asks for budget and timeline up front, so the free-text questions people add afterwards are a rare, honest signal.
insight: Group the questions by where people are moving from, and the worries become specific
mechanics: An aggregate, de-identified count of questionnaire questions by origin market, with no lead-level data.
Rachel's answer to the top three, in her own words.

outcome.gap: The de-identified aggregate hasn't been pulled yet, and Rachel hasn't chosen the three questions.

takeaway: The question someone asks last is often the one they should have asked first.

cta.text: Moving to South Florida? Start with the home-match questionnaire.

evidence.summary: The Fit Finder flow collects budget and timeline before submission; the question aggregate itself does not exist yet.

sensitivity.notes: Rachel's voice. Distribution of Rachel-identity posts belongs to RachelOS #1036/#333; this entry only tracks the candidate.

commercial.rationale: Real estate inquiries for Rachel; no TKO offer applies.
